It then joins this result back to 't5' to find all 't5.c1' (bars) that offer that specific minimum price for that 't5.c2' (beer), and finally joins with 't1' to get 't1.c1'. This means Q1 will only return rows corresponding to the absolute lowest price for each beer, and all bars offering that lowest price. Q2, on the other hand, performs a LEFT JOIN between 't2' and 't5', and then groups the result by 't2.c1' (beer) and 't5.c1' (bar). It calculates the minimum 'c3' (price) for each unique (beer, bar) combination. The 'HAVING' clause filters out beers with no associated 't5' entries. Consequently, Q2 can return multiple rows for a single beer if it's sold by different bars, each with its own minimum price (which might not be the overall minimum for that beer), whereas Q1 would only show the bars offering the overall minimum price.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample demonstrates the difference when a 'beer' ('t5.c2') is sold by multiple 'bars' ('t5.c1'), and some bars offer the absolute minimum price for that beer, while others offer a higher price. Q1 will only list the bars offering the absolute minimum price. Q2 will list all bars selling the beer, along with the minimum price offered by each specific bar, thus producing more rows and potentially different price values for the same beer.
